preamble: Voicing of the voiceless alveolar affricate [ts] to [dz] is part of the Western Romance lenition of intervocalic consonants. The [ts] that arose from palatalized Latin c before front vowels and from -TY- clusters was voiced between vowels in medieval Ibero-Romance. So Old Spanish and Old Galician-Portuguese contrast intervocalic voiced z [dz] (dezir, vezino) with voiceless ç [ts] that comes from geminates and post-consonantal positions (caçar, calça).

examples.from: Vulgar Latin vĭcīnum, intervocalic palatalized c > *[ts]
examples.note: Intervocalic /dz/ is the reflex of an earlier /ts/ that was voiced; it later became [ð] and then [θ] (modern vecino).
The voiced affricate later deaffricated to modern Portuguese [z] (dizer [dʒiˈzeɾ] in Brazil).

sources: Mackenzie, I. (n.d.). History of Spanish Consonants. Newcastle University. https://www.staff.ncl.ac.uk/i.e.mackenzie/consr.htm
Penny, R. (2002). A History of the Spanish Language (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511992827
